entities.title: Whole-file reads, not mmap
entities.summary: Files are read into a buffer with read(2); mmap is deliberately not used.
entities.context: `afs serve` and `afs jsonl` are long-lived processes that read files other programs may be editing at the same moment.

options.title: mmap
options.consequences: No copy, but truncating a mapped file while it is read raises SIGBUS and kills the process.

options.title: read(2) into a buffer
options.consequences: One copy per file; a file changed mid-read gives stale or partial bytes, which the stamps and the racy window catch, never a crash.

entities.decision: Read whole files with read(2). On Linux, open with O_NOATIME (retried without it when the kernel refuses with EPERM because the caller does not own the file) and hint posix_fadvise(SEQUENTIAL). Match with the regex crate and memchr, and walk searches with the ignore crate's parallel walker.
entities.rationale: Truncating a mapped file raises SIGBUS and would kill a long-lived server.
entities.origin: macos/rust/agent-fs/README.md, section I/O, before it moved here.

entities.title: Batched loading chosen by timing, per process
entities.summary: Each process times io_uring (Linux) or POSIX AIO (macOS) against plain reads on its first files and keeps the faster; AFS_BATCH_IO overrides it.
entities.context: Search and outline load many files at once. Batching is not always faster: with a hot page cache, cached opens and reads submitted to io_uring are punted to kernel worker threads, and plain reads measured faster on a small virtual machine (the README keeps the measurement).

options.title: Always batch
options.consequences: Slower wherever the page cache is hot and the kernel punts the work.

options.title: Never batch
options.consequences: Gives up the gain on cold caches.

options.title: Time both per process
options.consequences: The first 128 files of each method may be loaded the slower way.

entities.decision: fsio::load_many alternates the batched and the plain loader until each has loaded 128 files (TRIAL_FILES), then keeps whichever took less time per file. AFS_BATCH_IO=always or never forces one; anything else is auto. On Linux, uring.rs opens a chunk of files in one round (OpenAt), stats and reads them in a second (Statx linked before a 64 KiB Read, so the stamp is taken before the bytes; pread for the rest of bigger files) and closes them in a third; rings are pooled, probed for those opcodes, and any ring failure disables io_uring for the process. On macOS, aio.rs opens and stamps files one by one (macOS has no asynchronous open) and reads each batch of 16 with one lio_listio(LIO_WAIT) after F_RDAHEAD; empty files and files over 4 MiB use plain reads.
entities.rationale: Neither method wins everywhere, and the machine at hand decides which is faster.
entities.details: The README stated, before this section moved, that the AIO loader was type-checked against Apple's libc bindings and unit-tested in macOS CI but not benchmarked on a Mac.
entities.origin: macos/rust/agent-fs/README.md, section I/O, before it moved here.

entities.title: Stamps younger than 2 seconds prove nothing
entities.summary: A file's stamp is trusted to mean "unchanged" only once its mtime and ctime are more than 2 seconds older than the moment the stamp was taken.
entities.context: afs skips re-reading and re-hashing a file, and reuses cached results, when a file's stamp (device, inode, size, mtime and ctime in nanoseconds) is unchanged. A file edited twice within one timestamp tick, with the same size, keeps the same stamp.
entities.decision: Ident.racy marks a stamp racy when max(mtime, ctime) + 2 s is later than the time it was taken. A racy stamp never lets read skip loading the file, never makes a cached search, list or outline result reusable, and never keeps a trigram-index entry fresh; such files are always read again.
entities.rationale: The rule git uses for its index: same-tick edits cannot serve stale data.
entities.origin: macos/rust/agent-fs/README.md, section Caching, before it moved here.

entities.title: Staleness by re-stat, not file-system events
entities.summary: Cached results and index entries are checked by stat-ing what they depend on; no inotify, fanotify or FSEvents watcher keeps a dirty set.
entities.context: A session reuses search, list and outline results and trigram-index entries, and must notice files that changed since.

options.title: Re-stat every dependency on each hit
options.consequences: One stat per visited path on every repeat; no background thread and nothing platform-specific.

options.title: File-system event watchers
options.consequences: A repeat would touch only what changed; three platform APIs to support.

entities.decision: Re-stat. Watchers stay planned work, absent until a benchmark justifies them.
entities.origin: macos/rust/agent-fs/README.md, sections Caching and Not implemented, before they moved here.

entities.title: Build the trigram index from the second search, in memory
entities.summary: A session indexes a walk configuration only once a second search on it is computed, and keeps the index in memory, never on disk.
entities.context: Building the index costs reading every file once; a one-off search gains nothing from it.
entities.decision: TriIndex.warm returns true from the second computed search on a configuration; that search reads every file once, indexing and scanning in the same pass. The index lives in the session's State and is dropped with it.
entities.rationale: The code's own comment on warm: the index is worth building from the second search on.
entities.origin: macos/rust/agent-fs/README.md, section Trigram index, before it moved here.

entities.title: What may change in the request protocol and the MCP tools
entities.summary: Agents and the agent-fs skill rely on op, field and tool names and on reply fields such as unchanged, ref, hunks and next_ranges; nothing says which of them may change.
entities.context: The contracts in macos/rust/agent-fs/src/.dev/contracts.json are relied on by coding agents through MCP or a shell and by agents/skills/agent-fs/SKILL.md. The crate is at version 0.1.0 and the repository states no compatibility policy for them.

options.title: Additive only
options.consequences: Fields and tools are only added; a rename or removal needs a new name.

options.title: Change freely with the skill
options.consequences: Any change is allowed if the skill and the README change in the same commit; agents with older instructions may break.
